nameStory: These tiny clams earned their "peaclam" name because they're about the size of a pea when fully grown. The "Greater Eastern" part distinguishes this species as the largest of the eastern peaclams, though "greater" is relative - we're still talking about a clam smaller than your thumbnail!
description: The Greater Eastern Peaclam is a tiny freshwater clam that most people overlook completely. These mini mollusks have rounded, yellowish-brown shells that rarely exceed 6 millimeters (about a quarter inch) across. They're filter feeders that spend their lives buried in the muddy or sandy bottoms of ponds, lakes, and slow streams. Despite their small size, they're actually important players in freshwater ecosystems, helping to clean the water by filtering out tiny particles.

idTips.label: Shell size and shape
idTips.description: Look for a rounded, inflated shell about 4-6mm across - roughly the size of a peppercorn. The shell feels smooth and thin when you pick it up, almost fragile between your fingers.

idTips.label: Shell color
idTips.description: Fresh shells are yellowish-brown to pale amber, sometimes with a slight greenish tint. Old, weathered shells on the shore turn chalky white or gray.

idTips.label: Shell ridges
idTips.description: Run your fingernail across the surface - you'll feel fine concentric ridges that mark growth lines, like tiny tree rings on the curved shell surface.

idTips.label: Beak position
idTips.description: The pointed 'beak' or umbo sits slightly off-center toward one end, not right in the middle like a perfect circle would have.

idTips.label: Shell thickness
idTips.description: The shell feels surprisingly light and delicate for a clam - you can easily crack it between your fingers, and it's somewhat translucent when held up to light.

habitat: Look for Greater Eastern Peaclams in quiet freshwater areas throughout New England - ponds, slow-moving streams, lake edges, and even temporary pools. They prefer muddy or sandy bottoms rich in organic matter where they can burrow and filter-feed. You'll often find their empty shells washed up on the shores of lakes and ponds after storms.

seasonality.spring: Active season begins as waters warm. Look for tiny siphon holes in shallow, muddy areas near shore where they're filter-feeding.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most actively filtering and growing. Fresh shells with animals inside are most likely to be found now.
seasonality.fall: Still active but slowing down. Empty shells from summer mortality start washing ashore and can be found along waterlines.
seasonality.winter: Dormant in sediments under ice. Best time to search for weathered shells along frozen lake shores and stream banks.

funFact: These tiny clams are actually hermaphrodites that brood their babies - they carry developing young inside their shells like living nurseries, then release fully-formed miniature clams rather than helpless larvae!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with other peaclam species, which require expert examination to distinguish. Remember: if it's pea-sized, rounded, and found in fresh water, it's some type of peaclam. The Greater Eastern is typically the largest you'll encounter in New England.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Greater Eastern,' this is still a tiny creature that most people never notice. The entire family of peaclams is often overlooked by naturalists, but they're incredibly common and ecologically important in freshwater systems.
compareHints: Since this appears to be the only Pisidium species commonly reported in New England, compare it with other peaclam genera like Sphaerium, which tend to be more triangular and often larger. Greater Eastern Peaclams are more perfectly rounded and stay smaller, rarely exceeding 6mm while Sphaerium species can reach 10-15mm.
